title: Ledger of Numbered Accounts
statement:
Build a small ledger for n accounts numbered 1 to n. The constructor gets balances, where balances[i] is the starting balance of account i + 1.

  • credit(account, amount) adds money to an account.
  • debit(account, amount) takes money out of an account.
  • move(from, to, amount) takes money out of from and adds it to to.

Each method returns true if it succeeded. It must return false and change nothing if any account number is outside 1..n, or if the account paying out has less than amount. Moving money from an account to itself is allowed and leaves the balance unchanged.

Tests are a list of operations and their arguments; the first creates the ledger. The expected output has one entry per operation (null for the constructor).

examples.why: After the debit and the move, the balances are 20 and 45. Account 3 does not exist. Account 2 holds 45, one short of 46.
The move fails because account 2 does not exist, and nothing is taken from account 1. So the full 10 is still there to debit.

constraints: 1 ≤ account, from, to ≤ 100 001 (may be out of range)
hints: Accounts are numbered 1 to n. What is the simplest structure that finds a balance by account number in O(1)?
Every method starts with the same checks. Write a small helper that says whether an account number is valid.
Do all checks before changing anything. For move, check both accounts and the balance first, then subtract and add.

explain.intuition:
There is no clever algorithm here. The test is whether you write careful, defensive code. An array indexed by account − 1 gives O(1) access. The interesting part is the order of operations: validate everything, then mutate. If move subtracted from from before discovering that to does not exist, money would vanish.

This is the same discipline as a form submit handler: validate all fields first, and only then write to state, so a failed request leaves nothing half-applied.
steps: Store the balances in an array; account a lives at index a − 1.
credit: if the account is invalid return false; otherwise add and return true.
debit: if the account is invalid or its balance is less than amount, return false; otherwise subtract and return true.
move: if either account is invalid or from has less than amount, return false; otherwise subtract from from, add to to, return true.
pitfalls: Changing a balance before every check has passed, so a failed move still debits from.
Forgetting that accounts are 1-indexed: reading balances[account] is off by one, and account n looks invalid while account 0 looks valid.
Rejecting a balance that exactly equals the amount. Draining an account to 0 is allowed.

solutions.title: Array with validate-then-mutate
solutions.idea: Keep balances in an array. Each method checks account numbers and funds first, and only then changes balances.

solutions.title: Build on a single debit/credit pair
solutions.idea: Implement move as a debit followed by a credit. To stay all-or-nothing, check the receiving account before the debit runs.

followups: Many requests now arrive in parallel. How do you lock a move between two accounts without deadlocking when two moves go in opposite directions?
Add a history of transactions per account that can be listed newest first. What would you store?
